title: Interpreting Quantum Learning Models via Stochastic Processes
authors: Johannes Fankhauser, Lukas J. Fiderer, Hans J. Briegel
abstract: Quantum machine learning models define probabilistic input--output maps through coherent quantum evolution and measurement. While such models can exhibit computational advantages, their internal functioning and decision making generally resists interpretation in terms of stochastic trajectories through intermediate configurations. In contrast to classical (Markovian) stochastic processes, quantum dynamics generically violates the Chapman--Kolmogorov divisibility condition, preventing a decomposition into probabilistically meaningful intermediate transitions. We develop a probabilistic framework for representing quantum learning models as stochastic processes over configuration spaces where the dynamics are modeled as linear maps on probability distributions. Starting from a fixed POVM, arbitrary quantum channels induce transition kernels on the associated probability representation. For informationally complete POVMs, and in particular SIC-POVMs, these kernels are Markovian but generally quasi-stochastic, with non-classicality appearing as negativity. By contrast, projective spaces admit positive stochastic kernels but generally require non-Markovian dynamics due to the failure of Chapman--Kolmogorov divisibility. This yields a trade-off between negativity and dependence on past configurations, i.e. quantum dynamics can be represented either by Markovian quasi-stochastic maps or by positive stochastic processes with higher Markov order. We discuss how such representations of quantum dynamics can be interpreted as stochastic walks through a memory space in the spirit of Projective Simulation, a model of learning and agency in which decisions arise from random walks over an episodic memory network. We further outline how finite-order stochastic kernels can approximate such quantum deliberation processes and show in what regimes the classical machine learning model is recovered.
summary: The paper tackles the challenge of interpreting Quantum Machine Learning models by translating their unitary evolution into probabilistic stochastic processes. It reveals an inherent trade-off: achieving a simple Markovian description requires introducing negative probabilities (quasi-stochasticity), whereas maintaining strictly positive transition probabilities forces the dynamics to become non-Markovian and history-dependent.
main_problem: The core problem is interpreting Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, whose probabilistic mapping arises from coherent quantum evolution, because their internal dynamics resist description using classical stochastic trajectories.
main_result: A fundamental trade-off exists: representing dynamics via Markovian processes requires quasi-stochastic kernels with negativity (using IC-POVMs), while maintaining positive stochasticity necessitates non-Markovian dynamics requiring memory of past states (using Projective Spaces).
method: The authors develop a probabilistic framework mapping quantum channels to linear maps on probability distributions over configuration spaces defined by POVMs, comparing the mathematical properties of these induced kernels.
model_or_system: The model centers on QML circuits whose evolution is described by unitary gates followed by measurements characterized by a Positive Operator-Valued Measure (POVM). The analysis compares representations based on Informationally Complete POVMs versus Projective Spaces.
key_observables: Transition kernels ($T^i_j$), negativity of the kernel, Markov order ($	ext{L}$), and adherence to the Chapman–Kolmogorov divisibility condition.
important_parameters: The choice between IC-POVMs (leading to quasi-stochasticity) and Projective Spaces (leading to positive but non-Markovian dynamics).
main_assumptions: The analysis adopts a discrete-time description, and the comparison hinges on whether one prioritizes Markovian structure or positivity of transition probabilities.
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes, but the discussion implies comparisons (like Table I) summarizing the trade-offs between different POVM representations regarding stochasticity and memory order.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the difficulty of interpreting quantum dynamics stochastically due to C-K violation. It then develops a general probabilistic framework using POVMs, culminating in a detailed comparison showing the inherent trade-off between Markovian structure (quasi-stochastic) and positivity (non-Markovian).
why_interesting: This work provides a deep mathematical lens through which to view quantum computation's operational semantics, linking fundamental concepts like non-classicality directly to the failure of classical stochastic process assumptions.
